views.Latin: LIBER PRIMVS [I.1.1] Bello Parthico, quod inter Macchabaeos duces gentemque Medorum diuturnum ac frequens uariaque uictoria fuit, incentiuum dedit sacrilegii dolor, quia rex Antiochus cui nomen Illustris, Antiochi regis filius, ubi Aegyptum quoque suo imperio adiunxit, in superbiam elatus, quod ei incerta bellorum prosperauissent, ritus Hebraeorum neglegi mysteriaque eorum profanari iusserat, idque postulantibus plerisque Iudaeis statuere ausus. Compare with Bellum [I.1.2] Quod factum Matthathias sacerdos perpeti nequiuit, nec solum ipse temperauit a sacrilegio regalique edicto non obtemperauit, uerum etiam immolantem simulacris hostias de popularibus suis nanctus gladio transuerberauit. Et congregata manu atque Asidaeis in societatem adscitis ipse cum filiis suis temerantes usum patrium et iustitias legis alios necauit, plerosque expulit bellique sabbato adoriendi auctor fuit, ne simili arte ipsi quoque deciperentur, sicut iam plerique eorum, dum sabbato bellum suscipere detrectant, inruentibus in se hostibus inulti occubuere. Potentiam prosperi actus dederunt, et perseuerauit in uiro usque ad exitum uitae studium defensionis et pietatis uigor. Sed cum sibi supremum diem adesse intellegeret, uocatis ciuibus atque adsistentibus liberis hortatus est, ut tuerentur patriam templique religionem, ducemque his Iudam Macchabaeum curae ac sollicitudinis suae successorem reliquit. Compare with Bellum [I.1.3] Qui bello strenuus, consilio bonus ac prae ceteris fide promtus quam frequenter innumeras hostium copias parua manu fuderit, persequi non est negotii praesentis. Quod tamen breui colligere datur, saepe prosperis usus successibus excitauit in se magnam hostium multitudinem, qua circumfusus undique, dum cedere pudori existimat, refugientibus sociis in proelium ruit. Caesisque quos aduersum ierat, a latere circumuentus sed tamen ultus propriam mortem occiditur. Compare with Bellum [I.1.4] Huic successit Ionatha non minus uirtutis similitudine par quam naturae germanitate. Qui post multa in bellicis rebus opera, in rebus sacris officia, quae circa templi purificationem spectata ac probata sunt, praetenta per dolum amicitiae fide intra urbem hostium clausus nec longo post interuallo necatus est. Iohannes etiam senior natu frater et Eleazar iunior ceteris pro religione mortem non recusarunt. Compare with Bellum [I.1.5] Post hos rei summam Simon recepit, ad quam non rudis sed iam probatus fraternae societatis triumphis adpropinquauit, utinam et ipse tam perspicax ad fraudes cauendas quam manu ualidus bellandique artibus satis spectatus. Etenim cum uirtutis ope Romanorum ducibus regibusque gentium amicitiam foederauisset, Ptolomaei dolo generi sui rogatus ad conuiuium inter mensas et pocula cum duobus filiis qui aderant circumuentus atque exutus armis impiae neci traditur. Compare with Bellum [I.1.6] Sane praeuenit insidias Iohannes ortus ex Simone cui nomen Hyrcanus et properauit ad uicinae urbis moenia, ubi a populo propter egregia patris merita, odio quoque hostilis sceleris expectabatur. Vix denique ingressus urbem est, et iam Ptolomaeus aderat. Sed cum per aliam portam ingredi uellet, repulsus multitudini cedendum existimauit. Adsumsit ilico Ionathes paterni sacerdotii munus et a cultu rerum diuinarum profectus statim pietatis officia curamque seruandae necessitudinis exsequebatur, matrem cupiens fratresque periculo auferre. Compare with Bellum [I.1.7] Congressuque superior factus iustae passionis adfectu superabatur, quominus castro potiretur, in quo clausi adtinebantur. Nam Ptolomaeus ubi se urgueri uidebat, matrem eius atque germanos in muris locabat praecipitandos ilico, nisi Ionathes bello quod inferebat desisteret. Vincebatur iuuenis pietatis metu, qui uincebat fortitudinis adsumtione, et iracundiam excitatam in hostem reuocabat suorum misericordia. Mater tamen parata ad tormenta tendebat manus obsecrans non salutis auxilium sed ultionis solatium. Verebatur enim ne filius plus matri metueret quam paternae uindictae impenderet. Sibi mortem illam loco immortalitatis futuram, qua maritus uindicaretur et gener impius pro scelere immani poenam exsolueret. Sed iuuenis plus intra ipsum se quam in hostem proeliabatur; nam quotiens patrem cogitabat, accendebatur, rursus cum matrem uerberari atque ad necem aptari uideret, molliebatur. Reuocabat impetum, referebat gradum, quia retrahebat passio. Inter obsidionis moras feriatus ex lege superuenit annus qui erat septimus. Cessit pietas religioni, soluta obsidio. Sed eo magis Ptolomaei excitata immanitas, ut quorum obiectu pestem euaserat eos iugulari iuberet. Qui continuo se ultioni exemit ad Zenonem, cui nomen Cotylae, Philadelfiae regem confugiens, ut eius ope sese tueretur. Compare with Bellum [I.1.8] Nec Antiochus quieuit qui Simoni patri Ionathae ludibrio suos fuisse exercitus indignabatur, cupiensque adsurgentes adhuc Ionathae primitias extinguere, cum magna ueniens manu, Hierosolyma Hyrcanumque obsedit. Reppulit Hyrcanus auro, quem ferro nequibat, reseratoque, ut Iosephus auctor est, Dauid sepulchro tria milia auri talenta eruit, ex quibus trecenta adnumerauit Antiocho, ut obsidionem relinqueret, pretio emtus abiret. Atque ut facti inuidiam leuaret, fertur ea pecunia Hyrcanus instituisse primus xenodochia, quibus aduentum susciperet pauperum peregrinorum. Compare with Bellum [I.1.9] Aucupatus etiam Antiochi necessitatem, qua Medis bellum inferebat, ultus dispendium plurimasque urbes Syriae sibi adiunxit. Samariam quoque, ubi postea Sebastia condita est, circumdedit munitionibus, cuius expugnationem Aristobolo et Antigono filiis suis mandauit, quorum lenta obsidio usque ad diram famem et tetra alimenta humanorum cadauerum clausos coegit. Qua impulsi necessitate opem ab Antiocho, cui nomen Aspondius, petendam arbitrati ferentem adiumenta aerumnae societate implicauere. Victus enim a fratribus proelio fuga sese eripuit neci. Samaritani autem repentina obsidione captaque et euersa urbe seruitio dati. Quo rerum secundarum processu exciti Aristobolus atque Antigonus impetum non refrigebant, sed adiungere sibi finitimos bello coactos hautquaquam dissimulandum arbitrabantur : donec inuidia oborta bellum immane exarsit conspirantibus locorum incolis et coacta ualida manu. Quae tamen uicta profundam in reliquum tranquillitatem Iohanni exhibuit et sibi otium. Compare with Bellum [I.1.10] Hyrcanus trigesimo et primo anno longae quietis gratia functus diem clausit quinque liberis superstitibus, quod a plerisque beatitudini datur. Moderator egregius et pulchre sobrius, qui nihil umquam uel fortuitis euentibus dereliquerit, in quo actus eius offuscaretur, uxori summae rei commisit negotia, ipsam consultius ratus rebus publicis moderaturam, filios praescientia quadam animi tenens non diuturnos fore. Compare with Bellum
views.English: [I.1.1] Resentment at sacrilege sparked the Parthian war, which was long and repeatedly fought between the Maccabean leaders and the nation of the Medes, with victory passing from side to side. For King Antiochus, called the Illustrious, son of King Antiochus, once he had added Egypt too to his dominion, grew arrogant because the uncertainties of war had turned out well for him. He had ordered that the rites of the Hebrews be disregarded and their mysteries profaned, and had dared enact this at the request of very many of the Jews.Compare with Bellum[I.1.2] Mattathias the priest could not endure this. He not only abstained from the sacrilege himself and refused to obey the royal edict, but also came upon one of his own people offering sacrificial victims to idols and ran him through with a sword. Gathering a band and taking the Hasideans as allies, he and his sons killed some who violated ancestral custom and the ordinances of the law, and drove out many more. He also advocated taking up arms on the Sabbath, lest they too be deceived by the same device: many of them had already fallen unavenged when enemies attacked them, because they refused to engage in war on the Sabbath. Successful deeds gave him power, and to the end of his life his zeal for defence and the vigour of his devotion persisted. But when he understood that his last day was upon him, he summoned his fellow citizens and, with his children standing beside him, urged them to defend their homeland and the worship of the temple. He left Judas Maccabaeus as their leader, to succeed to his care and concern.Compare with Bellum[I.1.3] It is not the business of the present work to recount how often he, vigorous in war, sound in counsel, and keener than all the others in faith, routed countless enemy forces with a small band. In brief, however, this much may be told. After repeated successes, he roused a great multitude of enemies against himself. Surrounded by them on every side, he thought retreat shameful; as his companions fled, he rushed into battle. He killed those he had advanced against, but was surrounded from the flank and slain, yet not before avenging his own death.Compare with Bellum[I.1.4] Jonathan succeeded him, his equal in valour no less than his brother by birth. After many exploits in war and services in sacred matters, witnessed and approved in the purification of the temple, he was shut up in an enemy city under a fraudulent assurance of friendship and killed not long afterwards. John too, the elder brother, and Eleazar, younger than the others, did not shrink from death for religion.Compare with Bellum[I.1.5] After them Simon assumed supreme command. He came to it no novice, but already proved by the triumphs he had shared with his brothers. If only he had been as perceptive in guarding against deceit as he was strong of hand and thoroughly tested in the arts of war! For after his valour had won him treaties of friendship with Roman commanders and the kings of nations, he was treacherously invited to a banquet by his son-in-law Ptolemy. Amid the tables and cups, he was surrounded along with the two sons present with him, stripped of his weapons, and given over to impious slaughter.Compare with Bellum[I.1.6] But John, Simon’s son, called Hyrcanus, forestalled the plot and hurried to the walls of a neighbouring city. There the people were awaiting him because of his father’s outstanding services, and also out of hatred for the enemy’s crime. He had scarcely entered the city when Ptolemy was already there. But when Ptolemy tried to enter by another gate, he was repulsed and decided to yield to the crowd. Jonathan at once assumed his father’s priestly office. From the worship of divine things he proceeded at once to the duties of family devotion and the care of protecting his kin, wishing to rescue his mother and brothers from danger.Compare with Bellum[I.1.7] Though he prevailed in battle, rightful feeling prevailed over him, preventing him from taking the fortress where they were confined. For whenever Ptolemy saw himself hard pressed, he placed the young man’s mother and brothers on the walls, to be thrown down at once unless Jonathan abandoned the war he was waging. The young man, who conquered by summoning his courage, was conquered by the fear born of family devotion; pity for his kin checked the anger roused against his enemy. His mother, however, ready for torture, stretched out her hands, pleading not for help to save her but for the consolation of vengeance. She feared that her son would fear more for his mother than he would devote himself to avenging his father. Such a death would take the place of immortality for her, avenging her husband and making her impious son-in-law pay the penalty for his monstrous crime. But the young man fought more within his own self than against his enemy. Whenever he thought of his father, he flared up; then again, when he saw his mother being beaten and made ready for death, he softened. He checked his attack, drew back his step, because feeling pulled him back. During the delays of the siege, the year of rest prescribed by the law arrived: the seventh year. Family devotion yielded to religious observance; the siege was lifted. But Ptolemy’s savagery was all the more aroused: he ordered that the very people whose exposure had saved him from destruction should have their throats cut. He immediately put himself beyond reach of vengeance by fleeing to Zeno, called Cotylas, king of Philadelphia, to protect himself with his support.Compare with Bellum[I.1.8] Nor did Antiochus remain inactive: he resented the fact that his armies had been made a mockery of by Simon, Jonathan’s father. Eager to extinguish Jonathan’s power while it was still beginning to rise, he came with a great force and besieged Jerusalem and Hyrcanus. Hyrcanus repelled with gold the man whom he could not repel with iron. Opening David’s tomb, as Josephus attests, he took out three thousand talents of gold; of these he paid three hundred to Antiochus, so that he would lift the siege and go away, bought off by the payment. And to lessen the odium of the deed, Hyrcanus is said to have been the first to establish guesthouses with that money, to receive poor travellers on their arrival.Compare with Bellum[I.1.9] He also took advantage of the difficulties Antiochus faced in making war on the Medes, avenged his loss, and brought many cities of Syria under his control. He also surrounded Samaria, where Sebastia was later founded, with siegeworks and entrusted its capture to his sons Aristobulus and Antigonus. Their protracted siege drove those shut inside to dreadful hunger and the hideous diet of human corpses. Driven by this necessity, they decided to seek help from Antiochus, called Aspondius, and drew the man who brought them aid into sharing their misery. For, defeated in battle by the brothers, he escaped death by flight. The Samaritans, however, were enslaved when their city was captured and destroyed in a sudden siege. Spurred on by this course of successes, Aristobulus and Antigonus did not let their onslaught cool, but continued, by war, to compel neighbouring peoples to join them, until envy arose and a savage war flared up: the inhabitants of the region conspired together and mustered a strong force. Defeated, however, that force gave John profound tranquillity thereafter, and itself repose.Compare with Bellum[I.1.10] In the thirty-first year, Hyrcanus ended his days, having enjoyed the benefit of a long peace and leaving five children alive, something many count a blessing. An outstanding ruler, admirably self-controlled, he never left even chance events any opportunity to cast a shadow over his deeds. He entrusted the affairs of supreme power to his wife, judging that she would direct public affairs more prudently; he held, with a certain inward foreknowledge, that his sons would not last long.Compare with Bellum

And to lessen the odium of the deed, Hyrcanus is said to have been the first to establish guesthouses with that money, to receive poor travellers on their arrival.Compare with Bellum[I.1.9] He also took advantage of the difficulties Antiochus faced in making war on the Medes, avenged his loss, and brought many cities of Syria under his control. He also surrounded Samaria, where Sebastia was later founded, with siegeworks and entrusted its capture to his sons Aristobulus and Antigonus. Their protracted siege drove those shut inside to dreadful hunger and the hideous diet of human corpses. Driven by this necessity, they decided to seek help from Antiochus, called Aspondius, and drew the man who brought them aid into sharing their misery. For, defeated in battle by the brothers, he escaped death by flight. The Samaritans, however, were enslaved when their city was captured and destroyed in a sudden siege. Spurred on by this course of successes, Aristobulus and Antigonus did not let their onslaught cool, but continued, by war, to compel neighbouring peoples to join them, until envy arose and a savage war flared up: the inhabitants of the region conspired together and mustered a strong force. Defeated, however, that force gave John profound tranquillity thereafter, and itself repose.Compare with Bellum[I.1.10] In the thirty-first year, Hyrcanus ended his days, having enjoyed the benefit of a long peace and leaving five children alive, something many count a blessing. An outstanding ruler, admirably self-controlled, he never left even chance events any opportunity to cast a shadow over his deeds. He entrusted the affairs of supreme power to his wife, judging that she would direct public affairs more prudently; he held, with a certain inward foreknowledge, that his sons would not last long.Compare with Bellum
